items.title: Lesson 2, Investigate: Identify Crosscutting Concepts and Review the News (electron microscopes and atomic-scale technology)

body.html: These are open-ended activities with no single numerical answer.

Sample crosscutting-concepts table entries for an electron microscope: Cause and Effect (a higher accelerating voltage gives electrons more momentum, so a shorter wavelength and sharper detail); Scale, Proportion and Quantity (a 0.1 nm wavelength lets us see features much smaller than visible light can); Structure and Function (the wave nature of electrons is what makes the instrument work); Energy and Matter (electric potential energy turns into kinetic energy of the electrons). For Review the News, pick a recent article about a quantum or atomic-scale technology (for example, a new solar cell or a scanning microscope), check the source (author, date, evidence, whether it quotes scientists), and then summarize the physics for the class.

answer.html: Open-ended; the sample table entries and source-evaluation steps above show the expected approach.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 12 question: An X-ray photon has a wavelength of 0.0520 nm before it collides with an electron and 0.0544 nm after. Compare the wavelengths, and find how much energy the photon lost.

body.html: 𝜆= 0.0520 nm, 𝜆′ = 0.0544 nm. Find the photon's energy change.
𝐸= ℎ𝑐/ 𝜆. The photon's lost energy goes to the recoiling electron.
𝐸= 1240 eV · nm

answer.html: The wavelength is longer after the collision, so the photon has less energy. It lost about 1.1 × 10<sup>3</sup> eV (1.1 keV), which went to the electron.

check.html: A longer wavelength must mean less energy, and the electron gains exactly what the photon loses.

items.title: 25: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 180 V. Find its de Broglie wavelength and speed.

body.html: 𝛥𝑉= 180 V, 𝑒= 1.602 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> C, 𝑚<sub>𝑒</sub>= 9.11 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>31</sup> kg, ℎ= 6.63 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>34</sup> J · s. Find 𝑣 and 𝜆.
The electric field does work 𝑒𝛥𝑉, which becomes kinetic energy, <sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝑚𝑣<sup>2</sup> = 𝑒𝛥𝑉. Then 𝜆= ℎ/ (𝑚𝑣).

check.html: The speed is well below 𝑐, and the wavelength is about the size of an atom, as for typical electron-diffraction beams.

items.title: 26: A 72-kg sprinter runs at 9.5 m/s. (a) de Broglie wavelength

question.html: (b) Why does the sprinter show no observable wave behavior when running through a doorway?

body.html: Wave effects such as diffraction appear only when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the opening. A wavelength of 10<sup>−</sup><sup>36</sup> m is about 10<sup>21</sup> times smaller than a nucleus (about 10<sup>−</sup><sup>15</sup> m), and a doorway is about 1 m wide, so no diffraction can be seen.

answer.html: 𝜆= 9.7 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>37</sup> m
(b) The wavelength is immeasurably small compared with the doorway or any other opening, so no diffraction or interference can be observed.

body.html: 𝜆= 0.200 nm = 2.00 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> m; find 𝛥𝑉.
𝑝= ℎ/ 𝜆, 𝐾𝐸= 𝑝<sup>2</sup> / (2𝑚), and 𝐾𝐸= 𝑒𝛥𝑉.

check.html: A longer wavelength than the 0.0914 nm of Problem 25 means a slower electron and a smaller voltage (37.6 V is less than 180 V).

items.title: 28 (Challenge): A proton has a de Broglie wavelength of 0.085 nm. Find its kinetic energy in eV. Use 𝑚𝑝= 1.673 × 10−27 kg.

body.html: 𝑝= ℎ/ 𝜆, so 𝐾𝐸= 𝑝<sup>2</sup> / (2𝑚<sub>𝑝</sub>).

answer.html: 𝐾𝐸= 0.11 eV

check.html: An electron with this wavelength would have about 200 eV, and the proton is about 1836 times heavier, so its energy is smaller by that factor.

items.title: 29: A golf ball flies through a narrow gap, but electrons diffract in crystals. Why is the wave nature of the golf ball not obvious? Estimate the wavelength of a 0.046-kg golf ball moving at 60 m/s.

answer.html: 𝜆= ℎ/ (𝑚𝑣) and ℎ is extremely small, so the golf ball's wavelength (about 2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>34</sup> m) is far smaller than any gap it could pass through. No wave effects can be seen.

items.title: 30: Find the de Broglie wavelength of a neutron (𝑚= 1.675 × 10−27 kg) moving at 350 m/s.

answer.html: 𝜆= 1.1 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>9</sup> m (1.1 nm)

check.html: A slow, light particle has a wavelength a few times atomic size, so neutrons can diffract from crystals.

items.title: 31: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 45.0 V.

check.html: It is longer than the 0.0914 nm found for 180 V, as expected for a lower voltage.

items.title: 32 (Critical Thinking): Electrons are sent one at a time through two narrow slits and build up an interference pattern. A researcher adds a detector at the slits to learn which slit each electron uses, and the pattern disappears. Explain this with the uncertainty principle.

body.html: Knowing exactly where the electron is (which slit) gives up knowledge of its momentum, because the position and momentum cannot both be known precisely.

With no detector, the electron's wave goes through both slits and interferes with itself, and each electron lands where the probability is high. This builds bright and dark bands. A detector that finds the electron at one slit fixes its position there, and the measurement disturbs its momentum unpredictably. Without a definite two- path wave, there is no interference, so the bands wash out.

answer.html: Finding which slit the electron uses pins down its position and randomizes its momentum, which destroys the two-slit interference. Without the detector, each electron's wave passes through both slits and the interference pattern builds up one electron at a time.

items.title: 28 (Challenge): Proton with the same wavelength (0.14 nm); find KE in eV

body.html: 𝜆= 0.14 nm, 𝑚<sub>𝑝</sub>= 1.673 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>27</sup> kg (a standard value, not given in this module); find 𝐾𝐸 in eV.
Same 𝜆 means same momentum, 𝑝= ℎ/ 𝜆, so 𝐾𝐸= 𝑝<sup>2</sup> / (2𝑚<sub>𝑝</sub>).

items.title: 32 (Critical Thinking): How does the uncertainty principle explain double-slit interference patterns, even if photons or atoms pass through one at a time?

body.html: A particle is described by a wave that gives the probability of where it will be found. Knowing exactly which slit it went through would mean knowing its position precisely, which would change its momentum unpredictably.

If we do not measure which slit the particle uses, its momentum (and therefore its direction) is not disturbed, and the wave goes through both slits and interferes with itself. Each particle lands at one spot, but where it lands is governed by the interference probability. After many particles, the bright and dark bands appear. If we did measure which slit it used, the measurement would disturb the momentum enough to wash out the pattern.

answer.html: Because the position (which slit) and momentum cannot both be known precisely, each particle's wave passes through both slits and interferes with itself. Each particle lands somewhere according to that probability, so the interference pattern builds up even when particles arrive one at a time.
